name: The Curtis household — a name from the post office's letter lists
head: curtis_liman

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE RETURN, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The office's list of letters uncalled-for is a RETURN — its statement of what was still unclaimed on ONE day — and the paper reprinted one return over as many consecutive issues as it took, so the bound is dated by the return of June 1835 and not by the issue it was read in (T-0425). The earliest issue this project reads the name in is 1835-07-01, 1 day later; that gap is an accident of which impression an extraction pass reached, and it is not evidence. Somebody was writing to this name at Chicago by 1835-06-30 and at no stated time before it; nothing says when they came. The date lines the printings set, and how they were weighed, stand beside this rule in tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py.

arrival_year.note: DRAWN, NOT READ. The household's arrival block holds a BOUND — somebody was here by 1835-06-30 and no source says when they came — so the year is drawn from the arrival years the known layer records, truncated at that bound and renormalised. It says what a household of this bound most likely was, and nothing whatever about this household.

persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Curtis, Liman' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 4 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1).

resident_research.summary: No reliable record outside the Chicago post-office lists could be tied to Liman Curtis with a date, place, occupation or kinship discriminator. The repository's own crosswalks record the refusal: The surname 'Curtis' is in Fergus's death notices and no entry under it carries the initial 'L' of 'Liman Curtis'. A surname-only agreement is a refusal, here as everywhere: the list prints eleven Smiths. This is a documented no-corroboration result, not evidence that the person did not exist.
resident_research.notes: Research only. Later-volume readings are recorded here and NOT promoted: T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply.

merge_ruling.for_merge: The initial L agrees with 'Liman', an uncommon forename, and the two returns are six weeks apart — 20 May 1835 and 1 July 1835, the scene date.
merge_ruling.against_merge: TWO RETURNS, AND NEITHER SETS BOTH. 'L. G. Curtin' is on the return of 20 May 1835 (#c013), 'Curtis, Liman' on the return of 1 July 1835 (#c004). No return sets both spellings. Neither card is an anchor: T-0483 and T-0510 both closed no_corroboration, and T-0510 recorded that Fergus's death notices carry the surname Curtis with no entry under it bearing these initials. BOTH SPELLINGS ARE POPULATED: the town holds curtin_david beside curtin_l_g and curtis_jacob_s beside curtis_liman, so neither surname is a stem only one man bears. And the fold would have to take the middle initial G on trust, since 'Liman' prints none. D6.

merge_ruling.for_merge: The initial L agrees with Liman and both cards are Chicago readings of the summer of 1835.
merge_ruling.against_merge: ONE ISSUE SETS BOTH SPELLINGS IN TWO DIFFERENT COLUMNS, WHICH IS EVIDENCE AGAINST AND NOT FOR. The Democrat of 1 July 1835 prints 'Curtis, Liman' in the post-office return at column 4 and 'L. Curtiss' at column 13 of the same issue. A compositor who set Curtis in one column and Curtiss in another that day was distinguishing two names, not wavering over one; C9 asks for a printing caught setting both spellings FOR ONE MAN and this is a printing caught keeping them apart. L. G. Curtiss is besides set 'L. G. Curtiss' on 22 July and 'Curtiss, L. G.' on 5 August 1835, three settings that never drop the second s, and the town holds curtiss_j beside him. The middle initial G is printed on the Curtiss side and absent on Liman's. D7.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE LETTER LISTS (T-0378, T-0379). THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER, NOT AN ARGUMENT: every other record here argues for a household, and this one argues for a PERSON. `data/residents/` cannot carry a person outside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing — one member, no dwelling, no division, no trade, no family, no arrival beyond the paper's bound. tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py derives the set and prints every refusal, `--gate` proves no record here gained a roof, a trade or a second member, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L214 carries the change of scale.

surname_collision.refusal: the town already names a Curtis
surname_collision.note: A COLLISION SAID, NOT ACTED ON. Run against the tree as it stands, this pass would not MINT this card: refusal 7 — 'the town already names a Curtis' — lands on it, because Jacob S Curtis (hh_curtis_jacob_s) already holds the family name Curtis. The owner ruled on 2026-09-18 (T-0660, option (c)) that refusals 7 and 8 are MINT-TIME rules: they decide whether a new household may be minted on a family name the town already spends, and they do not un-mint one that already stands. So this record is not retired, its id is not redirected at anybody, the town's population does not move, and the research row and directory matches it carries are not stranded on a retirement nothing draws. What has changed is that the collision is legible: a reader sees both cards and why both are here. REFUSAL 7 IS NOT A CLAIM THAT TWO RECORDS ARE ONE PERSON — it is the precedence rule between this pass and the ones above it, which give a man the papers gave a trade the family name a letter list only spells. Two of the collisions this reading uncovered are two different men. The pass's `rank()` is unchanged and the cohort is not re-derived; that was option (b)'s cost and the ruling declined to pay it. The derivation behind this block, both readings side by side, is docs/RESEARCH/letter-list-surname-collisions.md.
